Understandability and Coherence.explanation: I thought this story was very well crafted, all elements make sense, and as the story goes on, more and more details are revealed so that we get a full and complex picture of the relationship between the mother and daughter.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: I can't say that the story relied on sophisticated use of idiom, metaphor, or allusion. The strength of the language of the story are the ways that details evoke feelings, and give hints about the history of the relationship between these two people.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending was very good. The story was wrapped up by the end of the visit, but the mention of the next visit, when the mother was in the hospital lets us know that the visits will continue into the future, but also reminds us that that the mother is elderly and that she doesn't have unlimited time left. The mention of the gooseberries gone bad, which the mother had mentioned as being in season earlier, was a very nice detail on which to end the story.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing of the story was very good. Nothing felt rushed, or too stretched out. We got a feel for the visit, what the apartment was like, and how the mother probably spends a lot of her time.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: I also thought the balance here was very good. The author does a great job of inserting little details into the scenes that help the reader understand some larger truth about the lives of the characters and their relationship. For example, "her slightly sloppy movements those of someone used to eating alone." Another example: "'Paulette brought me some gooseberries. You wouldn’t believe how good they are. It makes sense, since they’re in season. Remind me to give you some before you go.' Paulette—a former neighbor who was my age—came to see her every week; she had never left C.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The revelation of the troubled relationship when the daughter was younger was surprising, but also felt appropriate. As we grow older, we want to be dutiful and kind to our elderly parents, but the hurt feelings from youth never really go away. The author does a good job of revealing this dimension of the relationship in a way that the reader isn't expecting.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: I thought I understood the narrator's perspective, but also that of the mother as well, through the details in the scenes, and from what the narrator reveals. For instance, "At the same time, she was firing off questions about my trip, the children, the dog. She didn’t answer mine. Afraid of being boring, always, when speaking of herself." Another example of this is the passage "She tried to come up with more subjects of conversation, so that I wouldn’t go too soon, leaving her alone with her desire for me, her longing to live with me, her daughter, forever.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I thought there was good balance between the narrator's description of the surroundings and the action going on, with her own thoughts. This is done in this instance when action prompts a memory in the narrator: "I took the shortest route to the train, the one that goes past the Shell station. There, in the old days, I’d stop to prepare myself for her interrogating look when I returned from the cinema, bracing myself, wiping off what was left of my lipstick. What will people think of you?

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The form and structure do not seem original. Yet the story is very compelling nonetheless.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I think the story prompts the reader to consider the ways that parent-child relationships change over time, and how those relationships are always laden with the feelings and expectations of the past. The reader feels for the mother, in her loneliness and desire to hold on to her daughter. However, she is not a completely sympathetic character either. The relationship feels very realistic.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The writing seems original, and does not use cliches.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There is a lot of good detail that brings the world alive in this story. Some examples: "At Motteville, we sat in the station for a long time. It was hot. It was quiet, both in the compartment and outside. I looked out the open window; the platform was empty. On the other side of the S.N.C.F. railroad barriers, the tall grass almost touched the lowest branches of the apple trees"; "The TV was on without sound, just the test pattern on the screen"; " I’d never seen her move her body in a natural, relaxed way; she never ran her fingers gently through her hair, never slipped a hand inside the neckline of her blouse while deep in a book. Her only gestures of abandon were expressions of fatigue: stretching with her arms above her head, slumping in a chair, her legs out in front of her. Less hardness in her face than there had been, less of that tension you need to make your way through life.

Character Development.explanation: Both characters feel complex and well developed. This paragraph manages to reveal a great deal about both characters at once: "While looking for napkins, I found a stack of romance magazines at the back of the buffet. I didn’t say anything about them, but she guessed that I’d seen them. "Those little magazines—Paulette gives them to me, otherwise you know I wouldn’t read them. That’s all she reads, these little stories about nothing. Still afraid that I’d criticize her reading habits. I almost said that it didn’t matter if she preferred Nous Deux to the Malraux she’d just borrowed from the public library. She would have been unhappy if I’d seemed to think her incapable of reading the kind of thing I read." There is so much subtle suggestion of judgement and assumptions, and unspoken thoughts that pass between two people who know each other well in this paragraph.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: I thought there is a great deal of complexity below the surface. The past is lurking underneath everything that is said and unsaid between the mother and daughter: "Her gray eyes, which had always suspected the worst of me, were fixed on me with a hungry softness. She had been counting the days, had told herself in the morning that this was the day I was coming, and there we were, the two of us, and half our time had already passed. The tone of our visit was playful and kind. The other tone, the violence from when I was fifteen, would not return.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Much of the story rambles in a redundant way. It isn't clear what the narrator and his mother share specifically, and much of the story feels vague and uninteresting. The narrative also seems to recount the mother's death twice.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story does not make sophisticated use of language. Metaphors tend to be either cliche (e.g. "Our small town, once the backdrop of our story, became a beacon of hope and resilience") or strange/inappropriate (e.g. "Each change brought new stories and memories, etching themselves into the tapestry of our lives.")

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending was much too drawn out, it just seemed like the same thoughts were repeated again and again: the narrator loved his mother, her memory stayed with him, her memory, they shared laughter and tears, etc.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: Time proceeds vaguely ("though the seasons," "days turned into months"), and so a lot of the action seems to be disconnected from time.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The scenes require more detail to make them interesting, and without the details about the relationship between the mother and the narrator, the narrator's thoughts seem vague and not interesting. For example, "We spent hours immersed in conversation, swapping stories and reminiscing about the past. As we laughed and shared memories, time seemed to stand still. Every word and every laugh echoed through the walls of our shared history, creating new memories to cherish." What did they talk about? What were the memories?

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The main turn in the story was not all that surprising, i.e. that the mother became ill and had to go to the hospital. It was appropriate to the story. And yet, we don't really know what was wrong with her, apart from a vague reference to the sun, nor do we know how she recovered.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The main perspective is that of the narrator. We don't get the perspective of the mother at all.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Without any details about the lives of these people, the narrator's references to joy, laughter, tears, and memories seem vacuous and without any emotional depth.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The form and structure are not original.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: My takeaway was that the narrator loves his mother, saw her through an illness, was joyous she recovered, and now is recording her death. I was not invested at all in their relationship or in either of their lives.

Originality in Thought.explanation: There are a lot of vague and cliche passages. For example, "The stories from its pages filled the room, intertwining with the memories of our shared past"; "The remnants of our last visit held no sadness or regret, but rather served as a reminder of the resilience of the human spirit, of the power of love to transcend even the harshest of realities"; "Each change brought new stories and memories, etching themselves into the tapestry of our lives. We shared laughter and tears, celebrations and challenges, drawing strength from each other's presence.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The physical world is not well developed. There are not many details about what things look and feel like. Some details are mentioned too many times. We are told the streets have cobblestones no less than six times.

Character Development.explanation: The characters are not well developed. The story would need to include more details about the conversation between the characters, and more detail about the history of their relationship.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: The story is quite vague and flat. There does not seem to be much meaning below the surface narrative.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story starts off very strongly, there is a lot of detail and we get to know some specific things about the mother, and her relationship with the narrator. However, the story begins to get vague and lose its direction when we get to the paragraph that begins "As the days wore on, I found myself struck by a profound revelation, one that lingered with me long after the visit had ended." The point of this paragraph is not clear, and the story seems to lose its focus after this point.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: I think the story is successful in the way language is used in the first half, but the language becomes vague and cliche in the second half. For example, this passage evokes a clear sense of the mother's appearance, movement, and personality: "She was in her morning wrapper, a cashmere shawl draped around her shoulders, the drabbest of slippers on her feet, and she wore this disarray with the preoccupied ease of royalty at home, leaning with one hand on the cane she had only recently begun to use, and waving the other with the flick of an archduke's plumes in my general direction." However, by the end of the story, we have a vague and cliche passage like this one: " A promise of company and protection even in life's most turbulent times; a bond of love as unwavering as the passage of the sun across the sky.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending felt vague and unsatisfying, and without the sharp focus on the specific details of the mother's character that we have in the beginning of the story.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing is good for the most part, although near the end, the actions and thoughts of the narrator seem to become detached from the passage of time. What happened to the mother? Is she dead? Is she still in the hospital? It would be okay if it was left ambiguous, but the problem is that the mother as a person in the world, rather than as a memory or a symbol, seems forgotten.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: I think the action of scenes and the exposition of the author are balanced well in the first half of the story, but that what was actually happening gets obscured a bit by the end. We have mostly the narrator's reflections here at the end.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: I think the main turn, that the mother suffers sunstroke and the house loses its warmth and maternal presence is both surprising and appropriate. The way that the language of the doctor's letter is included is effective in helping us understand what the narrator might have felt when they found out; we are not just told that it happened by the narrator.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We only have the perspective of the narrator, although there are some details that hint at the mother's perspective, e.g. "I saw the familiar hangings intermingled with samplers and Japanese screens in their unaltered niches, all of which had borne witness to the endless progression of hours, days, and years ticking away beneath the portrait of my father.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I think there is good balance through the story. The way the narrator leads the reader through the house when he returns and the mother is gone, all the while sharing his thoughts about how it feels, is interesting and done well.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I don't think the form or structure are original.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I don't think the reader is left with much of interest to ponder by the end. Again, the focus of the story peters out by the end, which is disappointing. The main idea seems to be the narrator's sense of loss and nostalgia.

Originality in Thought.explanation: For the most part, the writing seems original. However, it tends to become vague and cliche by the end. An example would be the last paragraph.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story does include plenty of good details that make the physical world believable and interesting. For example, "She was in her morning wrapper, a cashmere shawl draped around her shoulders, the drabbest of slippers on her feet, and she wore this disarray with the preoccupied ease of royalty at home, leaning with one hand on the cane she had only recently begun to use, and waving the other with the flick of an archduke's plumes in my general direction"; "I saw the familiar hangings intermingled with samplers and Japanese screens in their unaltered niches, all of which had borne witness to the endless progression of hours, days, and years ticking away beneath the portrait of my father.

Character Development.explanation: I thought the author did a good job of developing the mother as a character in the first part of the story, along with the narrator.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This story does not have the same kind of depth and nuance that Story 1 in this set has. The main difference is that the history of the relationship between the mother and child is not as complexly developed as in Story 1.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: This story makes sense as a coherent whole, nothing really seems out of place, with the exception of this small detail: The daughter returns a month later after her mother has fallen, and the dishes from her last visit are still in the sink. This suggests the mother fell the day of or after the daughter's last visit a month ago, but it also seems unlikely that she would have waited a full month to visit her mother after such an accident.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The story doesn't make sophisticated use of these literary devices, but neither does the story seem to suffer much from it. Toward the end of the story there are some expressions that seem out of place or inappropriate, e.g. "The hours stretched quiet and bittersweet, as if a stopwatch had been set ticking down in the background";  "Memories I would carry with me always, in the stained-glass corridors of my heart.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending seems natural; it makes sense that the story would end with the mother's death, and the aftermath is not too drawn out.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: I thought the pacing was good, the passage of time does not seem too compressed or drawn out. The one exception is the detail I mention in my response to the first question.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: I thought there was a good balance between the action and conversation in the scenes, and the narrator's reflections and thoughts.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The mother's accident is a surprise, but it also seems realistic and believable as something that someone with an elderly parent would need to confront.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: I think we don't get much perspective other than that of the narrator.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There is good balance between the details of the action and the surroundings, and the thoughts of the narrator. There are some places where more details would help to understand the characters' relationship better. For example, this passage: "When nightfall came we made popcorn and watched old movies we had memorized, line by line, commenting and giggling over forgotten details. We stayed up talking until the early hours of the morning, catching up on all the little details, big and small, that made up the fabric of our daily lives." Details are mentioned, but we don't know what they are.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The form and structure are not original.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The takeaway from this story does not seem particularly unique or original. The details create a realistic character in the mother, but as a reader I didn't feel that there was much going on here beyond the joys shared between the mother and daughter. There doesn't seem to be much of a back story to give it depth. Hints of a history, for example with photos of the father, are not developed.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The writing does seem original, and does not rely on cliches.

World Building and Setting.explanation: I thought this story does a good job in creating a world with a lot of specific detail, such as "The diner where Mom and I always stopped for pie after school—Mom always got apple, I always got cherry. The movie theater where I had my first kiss at 15, with Danny McPhee in the back row. The corner store that still boasted the same vintage peppermint-stick candy in its window that Mom would buy me as a treat when money was tight but joy was abundant"; references to the crossword, the details about the garden, and the food they ate.

Character Development.explanation: I felt like both the mother and daughter characters were developed well. Depth comes from the narrator's own thoughts and interpretations, and we learn a lot about the mother's character from the details about her home, her crossword habit, and her cozy shared activities with her daughter.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: I didn't feel like there was much going on below the surface narrative here. Much like Story 3, it lacks historical depth; there is no back story, details from the past, that would lend additional meaning to the actions we observe in the story.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: It follows a logical progression and builds emotion and narrative through the layering of details, allowing the reader clear signposts of meaning. The ending connects to the beginning—indeed, it creates a kind of looped narrative, a return, a change, and the failure of the first narrative, to connect, as symbolized in the gooseberries.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: It deploys literary devices subtly and cleanly. The gooseberries in the final paragraph are the clearest example—an image is set up and then returned to, encapsulating both the narrator’s relationship with her mother and the broader narrative trajectory itself. Largely, the story follows the broad conventions for contemporary literary fiction. The prose is spare and the moments of flourish usually relegated to splashes of imagery, like how the “tall grass almost touched the lowest branches of the apple trees” in the first paragraph.

Narrative Ending.explanation: As I said above, the image in the final paragraph connects to one of the culminating images in the story and restates the opening, creating and closing a loop.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The narrative displays a very adept sense of pacing. It shows this perhaps most keenly when it slows down before the shift in tone on page 2 when the narrative complicates the narrator’s relationship with her mother.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Like many dialogue driven stories, this piece uses dialogue as a means to dip into and out of the scene—transitioning into the narrator’s memory, summary, or internal monologue and then pulling the reader back into the moment as needed.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The most striking example is on page 2 with the shift in the narrator’s relationship with her mother. The intrusion of profanity explodes the story and our understanding of that relationship, it introduces complexity into the world of the narrative.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: It depicts a complicated relationship between the narrator and her mother. Both have clear love for each other and yet also there is a kind of underlying grief which neither can shake the other of. The mother needs the daughter more than the daughter can bear and there is no easy solution or answer.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: For the most part, the story maintains an external position. It depicts the narrator’s internal life through her vision of her mother, which is to say through her description of her mother’s life. This tendency is effectively broken at the bottom of page 3: “This time, once again, I felt that I was leaving badly, in a cowardly way.” These moments where the narrator speaks clearly about her internal state are paced such that they are emotionally heavy for the reader.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: While I would probably say that this is a conventional piece of contemporary literary fiction and it follows the genre tropes therein, it nevertheless avoids a three act structure and neither provides a clear resolution nor an obvious moral or anything like this. It is a subtle piece of fiction, written to be murky and painful. I might find it conventional from my vantage point, but a different reader likely would not.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Again, this is, to me, a conventional piece of contemporary literary fiction. It does not feel hugely original to me in theme or content, insofar as it follows conventions for literary fiction—it is murky, grey, and reads like a howl of grief. Still, there is a challenge here and a pain here which feels as though it is coming from a distinctly original place.

Originality in Thought.explanation: While much of what is being depicted here is standard ground for the genre, it proceeds in a way that avoids clear cliches or tropes and follows what is murky and painful. There are no answers here, and no easy endings. It also avoids using hackneyed language or imagery to force emotion out of its reader, relying on the now-standard tools of literary fiction to build a scene and cooly push the reader into feeling.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story proceeds with a close eye to detail. It depicts smell, sight, taste, touch, and so on, through combination of its narration and in the dialogue and sometimes by contrasting these positions (internal and external). Much of the story is built through the description of the narrator’s mother and the environment she has built for herself.

Character Development.explanation: This story follows a trajectory of increasing complexity. It functions by adding complications to a scenario until those complications reach a breaking point (in my view this happens when the narrator leaves the mother and with the line again “This time, once again, I felt that I was leaving badly, in a cowardly way.”

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Very clear use of subtext. The most obvious example is the gooseberries at the end of the story, but throughout the piece the way the narrator describes her mother is also the way in which we understand the narrator.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The narrative loops three times. Each time it does, it loses power and becomes more hyperbolic.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The literary devices here are often over-the-top and cliched. For example, “The day slipped away like a whisper in the wind” or "“Together, we weathered the storms of life, finding solace in the embrace of the community that surrounded us". Often, these devices are employed directly on top of one another and it is overwhelming and frustrating for the reader.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The narrative loops three times. Though this could be interesting in an experimental way, it instead feels like it has failed to follow a logical path. It reintroduces the mother's death as though it hadn't happened already. For example, "When my mother's time finally came, her departure left a void in our small town and in my heart. Yet, I sought solace in the memories we had created, the laughter we had shared, and the love we had nurtured. She may be physically gone, but her spirit lives on" followed by "And then, one fateful day, my mother's time came to an end. The void she left behind was immense, a testament to the impact she had on the lives she touched. But in the midst of my grief, I found solace in the memories we had created, the love that had bound us together.”

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The narrative struggles to follow a coherent flow and has no clear sense of narrative time. Though the beginning of the story, perhaps I might refer to it as the first loop, occurs in-scene, I believe everything after it unfolds in paraphrase. Instead of slowing down, the narrative loops and repeats, maintaining its condensed narrative mode.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: As I said above, though the first loop maintains a sense of scene, the story largely stays in paraphrase afterwards and it feels like this paraphrase becomes increasingly broad as the story goes on.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There is a kind of structural unpredictability here in the way the narrative repeats, but it is neither satisfying nor coherent and it does not feel controlled. While this is intriguing as a narrative structure, it does not

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The issue here is that the voice has little specificity, it leans on cliche and the story struggles to use external description or internal focalization to allow the reader to intuit about its narrator. Rather, the perspective feels flat.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Likewise, the story's emotionality is stunted in this draft. Often, the story tells the reader what is going to happen before it happens. Then, after it happens, the narrator describes to the reader exactly what has occurred and what was thought and felt about without any subtlety. For instance, "I am reminded of the power of love. How it can transcend time and transcend even death. My mother may no longer be with me in body, but her spirit lives on in every act of kindness, in every moment of laughter, and in every memory we created together." This quote is just the feeling that the story is trying to conjure in the reader, but by stating it outright, it fails to make the reader feel it instead of think it.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I am a little torn in what to say here—the story does not have a conventional structure, but it also does not seem to be in command of what it does have. There is a lot that can be done with loops and repetition and though this story neither achieves those effects nor seems to be intentionally working towards them, it is something of an inspiring structure. Structurally, it reminds me very loosely of something like "The Early Deaths of Lubeck, Brennan, Harp, and Carr" by Jesse Ball, the possibility of layered feeling and dread remains, however unused and unexploited.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: While there are moments which remain moving—for instance, the line: “I hoped, prayed, that she could hear me, that the sound of my voice could somehow bring her back to me”—they feel cliched to the point that I feel as though I have read them before. The larger problem here is, I suspect, that the narrator never feels specific as a character, and instead much more like a broad sketch or an empty vessel.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The use of cliches is constant in this story. Some examples: "The bond we shared could not be severed by the cruel hands of time or the trials of life"; "...the walls of nostalgia that had surrounded us before would crumble beneath the weight of reality"; "Together, we weathered the storms of life..."; and so on.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story broadly struggles at creating a clear picture of its scenes and either avoids sensory detail, when it is in its summarizing or paraphrasing mode, or avoids specificity, when it does try to stay in-scene. For instance, "The rooms were filled with remnants of our previous visit, frozen in time" or "As we laughed and shared memories, time seemed to stand still". In neither of these instances are details given—what are the remnants? What are the memories? They are signifiers without depth.

Character Development.explanation: As with the scene-work, the characters are left vague and serve largely as empty vessels for the narrative, which is unfortunate because the narrative relies on the complexity and strength of its characters to find meaning. The issue, as I will describe in a moment, is that there is no real subtext to this story. Without any interplay between the way the narrator depicts herself or her mother and the way the reader reads the situation, without leaving anything unsaid, it is much more challenging for the narrative to find nuance within its characters or its narrative.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This is a story where what one sees is what one gets. The narrator more or less describes the emotions the reader should be feeling, just as she describes the emotions that she feels. For instance, "The void she left behind was immense, a testament to the impact she had on the lives she touched. But in the midst of my grief, I found solace in the memories we had created, the love that had bound us together"; "And so, we savored each moment, for we knew that our time together was a gift. The remnants of our last visit held no sadness or regret, but rather served as a reminder of the resilience of the human spirit, of the power of love to transcend even the harshest of realities"; "When my mother's time finally came, her departure left a void in our small town and in my heart."; "But it wasn't always easy. There were moments when the weight of the world seemed too much to bear"; and so on. While it is itself a hackneyed writing workshop phrase, this story struggles greatly in showing emotion to the reader as opposed to telling them. It is a strange reality to narrative and perhaps to life in general that feints and gestures can be more moving and communicate more clearly than outright statements.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story follows a clear logical trajectory, beginning with the narrator’s arrival at her mother’s house through to the first departure, the note from the doctor, and then the return to the mother’s house. For better and for worse, there are no unexpected repetitions and the structure proceeds as would be expected.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: While I find the choices here to be grandiose and displeasing, they are consistent and occasionally touch a kind of unexpected beauty. For instance, “…her small face peering out from beneath the wide white brim like a turtle's from beneath its shell”. The parts which I find frustrating I also have to admit do maintain some degree of consistent atmosphere. The line “I lifted her hand and clicked my heels together like a diplomat under presentation to the Court of a minor principality” aligns well with the broader depiction of their meeting, however annoying and over-the-top that depiction might be to me.

Narrative Ending.explanation: While the build towards the ending proceeds naturally, the ending itself does not find a satisfying conclusion—instead, it seems to reiterate the narrator’s decision to return home without finding a scene to put that return into. If I were giving advice on the story, it would be to spend a bit more time on the ending and provide more specificity on the sorts of memory and nostalgia that are drawn out from the return, as opposed to the overwrought and broad prose the story closes with in this draft.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: While I have some quibbles with the pacing, in particular the motion departing from the mother’s house the first time and then returning to it and speed with which the doctor’s note is introduced and then acted upon—it feels rushed to me—I can see the logic of the decisions that have been made. It feels more like a failure of execution than of intention. There are some other moments where the pacing is manipulated impressively. For instance, the transition out of scene and then back into it here: “I stayed with her for one week; during that time, we spent countless hours conversing, either in the soft warmth of the parlor or in the dim twilight of the fragrant garden after supper. There, she would sit wrapped in shawls, shielding herself against the damp evening air.”

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Again, the motion between scenes and summaries here largely feels sophisticated. The story struggles with the specificity of those scenes, but it does well in returning to scene and in shepherding the story along. The scaffolding is largely effective. It uses markers of time (“As the days wore on…”; “The week drew swiftly to a close”) as both a way to pace the story but also to enter into and out of summary. These are not always so effective or elegant, but they function.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The story proceeds more or less entirely as expected. It offers few complications to the relationship between the narrator and his mother, though the early impression the story gives of their dynamic is odd and intriguing. It does not follow through on those possible implications.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The narrator’s voice generally speaks what is meant and often says outright things that would be better implied. For instance, “The sunlight streaming through the open doorway lapsed into silence, heavy with the accumulated weight of all my years away from her.”  The narrator consistently uses a hyperbolic style of prose which does create a unified tone, but, in practice, this does not seem to suggest anything about the narrator in particular.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Though the subject matter is obviously emotionally charged, this is not a particularly emotional story. The narrative’s tendency to state outright the way things are without subtext, coupled with the grandiose prose, makes it difficult for emotional depth to be found. For instance, the narrator’s first departure: “Mother did her best to hide her sadness, of course, but I saw the quiet grief simmering below the surface as she waved me off down the driveway and back into the cold embrace of the vast world beyond.” This line effectively defangs what might have been a moment of emotional intensity.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The narrative follows traditional tropes. As soon as the mother is visited, it is clear that the story will be about her age and her potential death. Of course, the issue here is not the subject matter, but the way that subject matter is unfolded. No attempt is made to reframe this narrative in an unexpected way. Although, to be clear, the conventionality of the structure is not, to me, necessarily a statement on originality. What reduces the piece’s originality, for me, is that it does not use its structure to disclose or excavate something about the relationship that might otherwise be hidden. Instead, what is on the page is all there seems to be.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The closest the piece gets to originality is in the strange tone of the narrator’s voice and the formal and playful dynamic hinted at in the early conversation between mother and son, but this ultimately offers little insight and has no meaningful subtext. The story follows conventions and does little either to subvert them or to lean into them to the point that they break, into feeling or otherwise

Originality in Thought.explanation: There is not a great deal of thought here below the surface. Some of the prose suggests original thinking insofar as the images, however over-the-top, can feel imaginative, but they have little staying power. The topics the story is thinking about, which I took to involve, broadly speaking, grief and aging, are considered on the surface level only. The aging of the mother is sad, the narrator is sad about it, and so on.

World Building and Setting.explanation: Some attempts are made at creating sensory detail. I appreciate the possibilities of the exaggerated prose, but it is not quite specific enough to create a textured scene out of what it depicts. The space that it describes seems to change every time it is described. For instance, when the narrator returns to his mother’s house, the objects which he encounter have not been encountered before by the reader. The sense of permanence or grounding is missing.

Character Development.explanation: Again, the closest the story comes to character development is through the exaggerated tone of the narrator’s prose, but it neither evolves nor changes and very little substantive is revealed about the narrator or his mother.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Again, the prose here is initially intriguing and it creates what feels like a unified voice, however frustrating I might find it. The problem is that the story struggles to give that voice context or depth—there is no subtext, no second-layer to be uncovered. That failure is, I think, the primary failure of the story.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The narrative follows a clear trajectory and though the narrator’s second return home is a bit choppy and rapid, the order and flow make sense.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The prose is clean and simple. It is relatively sparse in its imagery and rarely leans heavily on obvious metaphors or similes. There are sentences which are beautiful in their simplicity: “Rain began to patter on the windows as evening fell, the soothing sound of droplets on leaves outside lulling us into contentment.” The prose feels, for lack of a better word, honest.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending logically follows the story that comes before it. Though it is a bit hackneyed and cloying—the crossword puzzle as an image feels obvious to me, though I suspect it would be a sophisticated inclusion for an AI—there is nevertheless a real pathos to it. The difficulty lies more in the rapid transition before the narrator’s second return.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: As I said above, he pacing is strong until the second return. “When I returned a month later, it was not for a pleasant visit but because Mom had landed in the hospital after a fall in the garden left her with a broken hip and wrist” is simply too fast of a transition—no time is given to the experience away from home or to adequately set up or solidify the initial departure.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Though the narrative relies heavily on summary, it is still capable of moving relatively elegantly into dialogue. I suspect this is because of the specificity of the environments and scenes it describes in its paraphrase—it convinces the reader that the paraphrase is lush and so dipping into it feels organic. Nevertheless, the story has difficulty settling into a scene and this could probably be improved in a revision process.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: Outside of the moment of transition I have already discussed, the motions the story makes are clear and subtle and the way it proceeds through the narrator’s first visit is elegant and exciting. The topic sentences especially are well-considered, not relying too much on any particular strategy.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The characters here are given very little opportunity to be anything other than sweet and kind, which makes the narrator, the narrator’s mother, and the relationship between them feel saccharine. As far as I can tell, there are no moments of complication or even meaningful conflict between the characters. This also limits the narrative’s power.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: While I desire significantly more emotional complexity, the story does an admirable job of focalizing the narrator’s experience through her internal monologue and creating our sense of her feeling of warmth for her mother through both statements of fact, but also through the way she describes her mother and the memories they share. It is this latter method which is particularly effective. To give an example, the tenderness of the line “heavy on the pickles” here conjures the sense of warmth that the rest of the paragraph then states outright: “I made us tuna salad sandwiches, heavy on the pickles, while Mom set out glasses of iced tea garnished with mint from her garden.”

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: This is a traditional structure for a story like this. It does not create unexpected moments and there is no sharpness, subversion, or subtext that I can discern. It is also distinctly imperfect in its deployment of this conventional structure—the rushed second return home is, again, a significant place where the story stumbles.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Because of the lack of complexity within the characters and their relationship to each other, it is difficult to feel that the story is meaningfully sophisticated in theme. Though honest and painful in its simplicity, the grief it depicts ultimately feels too simple to be real—grief is a howl, I think, not a sadness with an answer as it feels like it is depicted here.

Originality in Thought.explanation: I am a little bit torn on this because I believe that the story is specific enough to create some sense of emotion. But, in the end, it is difficult to overcome the sense that I have read this story before. Again, it comes down to the lack of complexity I see within the characters and the neatness of the ending, which feels, for lack of a better word, too “easy”.

World Building and Setting.explanation: It is not the most sophisticated story in how it builds its setting, insofar as it relies a bit more on proper nouns and brands than I might like—for instance, “The movie theater where I had my first kiss at 15, with Danny McPhee in the back row” or “The comforting smell of Chanel No. 5 and coffee enveloped me as her familiar laugh, as warm and sweet as blueberry pie, bubbled up“—but, nevertheless, it does so effectively. There is a particular place being described, however well or poorly, and I believe that is the intention of the story—to conjure a specific place. This is enough to convince me.

Character Development.explanation: As I said above, the narrator and her mother both feel caught in a kind of saccharine mode. There is no room for complication or complexity in this draft. This is the failure of the story.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: While this is not a particularly subtle story, the use of images like the crossword puzzles and the way the narrator describes the mother (as I talked about above) and the environment as a way to create a feeling which is not always outright stated give the narrative a degree of complexity. It is not the most impressive piece of writing in this respect, but there is some amount of complexity here.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Yes--this story is really quite satisfying in the way it holds together, building in tension and significance as it continues. It's a quiet story, fairly insular, and even for the patience that it exhibits, every bit of dialogue, every detail feels like it adds up to something important and real about these characters and their relationship.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: Yes; this test criterion was a little tricky for me for this story because the story itself has a formality to it, the feeling of translation. (Obviously I don't know that this was *actually* translated from a language other than English, but the syntax feels of another language, and the diction and register of the the narrator make it feel to me like the reader is getting it in translation.) At any rate, because of the formal feeling of the narrator's voice here--and even the ways the characters speak to one another--I didn't find a lot of idiom or metaphor to be had. But certainly nothing stood out as diverging from the tone or mood of the narrator's voice here, and what idiomatic language there was felt successful. A sentence such as "This time, once again, I felt that I was leaving badly, in a cowardly way" feels *just* askew enough in its phrasing ("leaving badly, in a cowardly way") that it sounds like translation--and translated beautifully, of course, and using vernacular believably.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Yes; ending on those gooseberries was a surprising and delightful move, and the feelings--masked and hidden and denied and pushed aside as they are, by both the speaker and the mother--are captured so beautifully in the mundanity of that final image of the gooseberries. It's as if, with that description, we can see the mother's hands tying the knot so that the gooseberries wouldn't spill on the daughter's trip home--such an everyday but caring action--and now we're seeing its "evidence" in her absence--and that the daughter finds the now-rotten fruit still tucked in the vegetable drawer a month later points to the ways the mother has aged and changed while living alone (though not cleaning out one's vegetable drawer isn't so remarkable in and of itself) and the hurried way the daughter leaves, the guilt, the mother's ruined hope, the way the past casts a shadow on the present.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: Yes, the pacing here is very well done. The writer's choice to suspend the reader in the (extended) moment of the visit itself feels quite right given the tension surrounding the visit and the mother's overt and stated desire for the daughter to stay. The writer's attention here to the paragraph is also key when it comes to the story's pacing; the way the writer keeps the reader moving through the story with very short paragraphs peppered in through the longer paragraphs is strategically handled, and the variation between the length of paragraphs does much to both pull us through the story while also "putting on the brakes" as the reader is forced to move in and out of multiple paragraphs.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Yes; this story feels memorable for its use of scene. Details and descriptions such as "Her eyes on her plate, her slightly sloppy movements those of someone used to eating alone" are specific enough to give believability and nuance to the character(s), but not so specific that we get mired in minutiae. There's a vagueness still present in "slightly sloppy movements [ ] of someone used to eating alone" and this, here, is one of its considerable strengths: The writer knows when to keep moving, to leave the "meaning" unstated (the narrator doesn't follow it with editorializing or telling us her guilt or whatever else about this) and therefore all the more present and real.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: Yes, and this is an area where the story is somewhat a "sleeper"; the writer's trust of the reader to make connections from what's laid out is much of what gives the writing here its charge, rather than big pronouncements or narrative happenings. For me as a reader, the turns here are interior and understated; the turns happen through information and backstory that's meted out patiently for the reader (e.g., "[t]he other tone, the violence from when I was fifteen, would not return" and the accompanying snippets of dialogue). It's as if the narrator has nothing but time for the reader, which contrasts beautifully with the impatience and dutifulness underlying the daughter's visit with the mother.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: Yes, and these characters are unlikeable and diverse from one another in very believable ways. Rather than a story about extremes of human experience, this story has characters and events that we know and understand--either intuitively or because we've been in a similar situation of guilt and responsibility, of wanting something from another person that their either can't or refuse to give, etc.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Yes, this is expertly done here as well. This relates to structure in part, too, but the way the writer blends scene and summary is so careful and balanced; a paragraph like the one about visiting old people's houses shows how seamlessly the narrator moves between exteriority and interiority As is the case in living as well, there's no "distinction" between what's happening and how the narrator is seeing or interpreting it; there's a natural-feeling movement from exterior to interior without feeling forced or, worst, feeling like we're only getting the exterior in order to give an excuse to get to the interior.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: Yes; here, as above, the story does a lovely job of constantly moving us back and forward, from the story's present back to the past and then forward again to "catch up"--and sometimes even moving into what will happen later in the visit to play around with the reader's sense of the narrator's perspective here. It's a hard narrative move to pull off, but I think it's done really well here. A few moments that show off the writer's ability to cover large temporal distances with blinding efficiency: "At the same time, she was firing off questions about my trip, the children, the dog. She didn’t answer mine. Afraid of being boring, always, when speaking of herself. Later, she repeated, as usual, "I’m fine here. Couldn’t be better and 'I have no complaints.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Yes, to be sure here--and one of the real strengths here, I'd argue, is the complexity of the "unique and original" idea we're left with; it's nuanced, and hard to distill to a simple phrase or statement. Because of this, it avoids the "moral of the story" trap that stories often fall into, where the reader feels hit over the head with the idea(s) we're "supposed to get" from the story.

Originality in Thought.explanation: Yes; this story--from its descriptions, its careful dialogue, its structure, and its overall patience--feels wholly original and avoids cliche, at the language and narrative levels.

World Building and Setting.explanation: Yes, and I love the seemingly easy way the writer handles this. The reader isn't overwhelmed with catalogues of description, but instead, the story moves similar to the way many good poems move--I'm thinking about Forche's "The Colonel" in particular here--by using restraint to its advantage. I feel confident that the writer here could have given us paragraphs and paragraphs of description that would feel right and true; instead, they only give us the exact amount of description that's needed to build up both the diegetic sound and point us, gently, toward subtext and meaning (e.g., "The TV was on without sound, just the test pattern on the screen.")

Character Development.explanation: YES. These characters--few as they are--feel real and naturally drawn, down to the ways the narrator's character sees the mother: "Last image of her: in the doorway, rounded arms framing her heavy silhouette in a yellow dress—her prettiest one, tight around the chest and the belly—a wide, fixed smile." Here, we see both the mother--looking like a real person we might see and know--and see the narrator through what she notices, includes, and how she feels about the mother. Artfully done.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Yes; as mentioned above, the author here uses all the elements at their disposal to make a story that positively oozes subtext, without letting it be *all* that there is. A moment like this is when the narrator says, "As she used to, she said, 'Every living thing is beautiful. She seemed to have forgotten that I was going to leave." The way the narrator moves from what the mother said, as she used to, right into not what it means, but what the narrator *thinks* it means about the mother, reveals crucial characterization for both the mother and narrator.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: No, this is a hard pass for me. There is pretty much nothing that seems to be satisfying about this story for me as a reader; there's no unifying feature to the story, and even the paragraphs themselves seem to somewhat haphazardly be put together. The trajectory of the story feels both unsurprising and unambitious.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: No. There are some metaphors, but they're really all cliches, and the idioms that are used seem...misused? I'm thinking specifically of the statement "[w]hen my mother's time finally came," which idiomatically would be a euphemism for her dying. I think that's what actually is meant by it, based on the rest of the paragraph that follows, but there's a narrative disjunction that doesn't seem purposeful that makes the idiom seem misunderstood or inappropriate. (This is just one example of when it was unsuccessful, but it's representative of a pattern of ill-fitting idioms and overdone metaphors.)

Narrative Ending.explanation: No, this is a miss as well. The first sentences from the final paragraphs themselves point to the sort of scattershot nature of the ending, seeming to throw endless platitudes to see what might stick (none did): "In the years that followed...," "And now, as I sit here...," "I will forever cherish our time in that small town," and "For in the end, it is through love that we find our purpose." There's nothing earned or natural to this ending: it feels forced and preachy and like it could be the ending to positively any story.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: No, the story doesn't show a skilled relationship between compression and stretching of time here. The possible ONE exception is that it does take 3 (tiny) paragraphs for us to get from entering the house the fateful time to finding the mother lying sick in bed. I'd argue that there's still almost no tension created (anywhere in the story), but this comes the closest.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: No; as soon as there seems to be a scene landed upon (finally! Something to hold onto!), the story settles right back into vapid explanations or summary. Take the small paragraph about finding the mother; what surrounds scene-making possibilities of footsteps/etc. is so fumbling that I'd argue it takes us OUT of a scene: the obvious "my anxiety mounting with every step," the cliche description of the mother as "frail and fragile like a bird with broken wings," the interesting but ultimately obscuring statement that "the sun had taken its toll on her delicate frame.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: No; narratively, the first visit with the mother is so idyllic that it seems clear the tension has to be introduced later, so then when the narrator returns and something bad has happened, it feels expected. And honestly, nothing else really "happens" in the story (except for the "surprise" that it seems like the mother dies, and then dies again, but that's a writing problem, not a feature of the plot).

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: No. The only reason anyone in the story is unlikeable is because the narrator speaks in so many cliches as to make the story nearly insufferable, but that's not a feature of offering diverse perspectives. And there's nothing convincing about much of anything here.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: No; there's an illusion that we get emotion from the narrator, but it feels like the simulacrum of emotion, or emotion as understood only in the brain and not in the body, if that makes sense. (Emotion from someone to whom emotions have been described but never felt.) Phrases like "Memories of our last visit replayed in my mind, the laughter and connection we had shared now haunting me, like a whisper of a distant melody" sound like someone trying to convince me that they felt...sad? rather than someone actually experiencing sadness.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: No. I will admit that the form and structure of the story are not, indeed, what I would have expected, but here that doesn't contribute to the story being successful.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: No, afraid not. The narrator really loved their mother, and she was amazing, and they shared a wonderful bond that lasted a lifetime. Perhaps some readers would take this as heartwarming (though I don't even think it gives that), but there's nothing here that would strike the reader as unique or original.

Originality in Thought.explanation: No--the story is so full of cliches that it felt a little like an exercise to use as many cliches as possible. Indeed, there are far too many to include here, and it would be to ill effect anyway. Cliches abound throughout--from the first sentence's "I was transported back in time" all the way to the final sentence's assertion, "And as I close this chapter of our story, I know that our love will endure, forever etched in the fabric of our small town and in the depths of my soul." Woof. This is painful.

World Building and Setting.explanation: No, this is a big no from me. Both the highs (e.g., "We witnessed weddings, births, and farewells, and through it all, our bond remained unbreakable") and the lows ("The rooms were filled with remnants of our previous visit, frozen in time") are unbelievable because everything that's mentioned by the narrator is SO general that it feels like the description of human life rather than life actually lived through the senses. There's also some sort of pragmatic/logistical weirdness at times in which the narrator says things that make neither actual nor figurative sense; the most egregious in my view is the sort of nonsensical "call back" to the problematic sun description from earlier: "The sun no longer posed a threat, for I was there to shield her from its harsh rays, to protect her from harm." What does this mean? The literal sun? (Has she no sunscreen, no hat, no sunbrella?) Some...figurative sun that hasn't been touched on yet, and never will be? If it's the actual sun, I don't understand what's happening; if it's a metaphorical sun, I don't understand what the metaphor connects to in the real world or stands for in the figurative.

Character Development.explanation: No, these characters not only aren't believable, but they don't believably undergo any sort of change or exhibit any evidence of being any more dynamic than a cookie cutter would be.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: No, there's not enough patience here to allow for subtext. There's barely enough patience to allow for surface meaning; yes, events are described, but we aren't let in enough to real emotion or description to be able to make meaning of what's happening. Instead, the narrator can barely go two sentences without summarizing feelings and collapsing those with the actions: "Overwhelmed by guilt for not keeping my promise, I hurriedly made my way back to her house." Instead, if the author exhibited even a little restraint and just said, "I hurriedly made my way back to her house" following what comes just before it, we'd be left as readers to read into (i.e., make meaning out of) the narrator's actions. We'd actually get to be witnesses or observers of the narrator for a moment, rather than being reminded every. bloody. moment. that there's a narrator! telling this story! Look at me! I'm a narrator! Let me tell you what it all means, how clever my comparisons are! Oy.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: No. The story itself moves at an all right clip for me as a reader, but the overwrought, faux-heightened diction of the narrator gets in the way of and ends up canceling out any successes that find their way here. As a result, and the fact that there's an otherwise unremarkable plot here, the story doesn't add up to something meaningful by the ending.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: No; although there are some idioms well used here (i.e., used in ways that feel believable for a speaker of English to use), there's a wavering quality to the narrator's assessments and observations, which makes it difficult for me to get a handle on who this narrator really is. His pomposity makes it so that idiomatic phrases don't come up too often (though a stray "mind's eye" comes across just fine), but the metaphors themselves fall flat at the level of cliche (e.g., the whole tapestry metaphor that gets way overused here).

Narrative Ending.explanation: No, the ending is too explanatory for that. Many central questions remain (for example, the possible red herring but still interesting inclusion toward the beginning, "and I assured her that I was well again," and the description that "she nodded slowly, bracing herself for what was to come, and turned to lead me into the house"), and it's clear with the ending that any possibility the story had for complicating our understanding of...something has disappeared.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: No. We're told that the "week drew swiftly to a close," and to the author's credit, we do get some scenic moments in the story (more on that in a moment), but in general, the writing itself belies what's being discussed. It's as if there's a mismatch between the narrator and the subject or something. Time in general in the story feels distorted because there's not enough happening in the story to keep it moving.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: No; as much as I find the pacing of this story to be dreadfully slow, I do think the author has some strongish moments in creating recognizable scenes. The after-dinner garden scene, with its use of the simple conditional, creates a sort of comfort of repetition and feels seeable when the narrator describes "she would sit wrapped in shawls, shielding herself against the damp evening air." Not bad, right? But overall, there story has a real plodding quality that even passing strong moments of scene can't mitigate.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: No, not particularly. The parts of the story that feel unexpected here are not a matter of narrative but instead about the unrelentingly affected voice of the speaker.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: No, although the narrator here is entirely unlikeable, it's not due to diverse perspectives being offered, nor is it a witting choice, I think.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: No, because of this insufferable narrator, the story offers very little by way of emotion, and because the external is mediated through this dreadful narrator, nothing in or out feels meaningful.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: Yes, ultimately, I think this story passes the test of (slight) originality in its structure. It starts in action, walks us up to the conflict (underwhelming as the stakes may feel), and then ultimately denies us the closure we might want, or even expect, here. Instead of ending on resolution of some sort, or answers, the story leaves us with more questions. Are these particularly generative, compelling questions? No. But I have to give the story credit for subverting our expectation that the story might be neatly closed by the ending.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: No, I'm afraid not. I had real hopes here in the beginning when the narrator remarks "I had not realized that the years of separation—years filled with bustling cities and the intense, absorbing world of sophisticated science—had invaded my memory and slowly remodeled her image into something almost fashionable." Neat! This feels unique and like a fascinating way to think about personal histories, and the ways our memory betrays us, focused as it always is by our present circumstances. But then, the narrator's perverse self-importance gets the better of him, and we suffer under sentences like these: "For as complicated as the tapestry of our intertwined lives may have been, and as diverse as our shared experiences often proved to be, it gradually dawned upon me...." Bleh. The narrator here is too clever by half, and the story struggles because of it.

Originality in Thought.explanation: No; and while I gain a peevish delight at the fact that being called "cliche" would likely be one of this narrator's worst fears, I am ultimately joyless at the overdone cliches here (some particularly icky examples include: "heavy with the accumulated weight of all my years away from her"; "fate, it seemed, had other plans for me"; and "confident in the belief that she would forever endure, an immortal anchor amidst the stormy seas of my journey.

World Building and Setting.explanation: No. Part of this comes down to a tendency of this narrator to heap on specific description (e.g., "the births of scholars who had not even considered their theses when I last stood in this room") or piling metaphor on top of metaphor (as in this mystifying sentence, bedeviling me to this very moment: "The town's picturesque streets were lined with flowers and fringed with dappled patches of sunlight, coaxing forth a murmur of echoes that dissolved under the soft glow of quaint lamplight"). I very well might be on board as a reader with some portion of that, but the layering of words and sensations ends up making the language itself somewhat meaningless. This overwrought quality again here challenges the reader to find footing.

Character Development.explanation: No, and this is where I feel we are fairly robbed in the story. There's a sort of unkept promise when, in the beginning, the narrator says "and I assured her that I was well again." That's some dang foreshadowing if I ever saw some! But never, ever do we see anything come of this; the mystery that could've grown--and added to this character's complexity and believability--is cut out at the root by the pretentious musings of this narrator. We all know pompous people, of course; but even the most conspicuously showy among us would be hard pressed to say "Calms, too, were restored upon the earth and in the heavens. What a strange experience it was to accompany my mother once more" while keeping a straight face. The narrator is a caricature, and the mother is merely an old mother, and that's that. (I also even had hopes for the letter-writing doctor! But alas.)

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: No; as above with characterization, again here we are denied subtext by this tedious narrator's recounting of the story. Describing the clock at the abandoned house of the now-infirmed mother COULD be a smart and subtext-building choice, but not when the narrator splashes all over the place to explain that "Its rhythmic cadence was as certain and unstinting in its duty as a soldier on march, serving as a sobering reminder that the world waited for no one, not even my mother." Boo hiss. Crushed, any hope for subtext here.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: No, this story doesn't accumulate to much. It's less of a story and more of an advertisement for nostalgia. As a result, few parts of the story feel authentic, either to real life or to a particular character.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: No, the story fails the test here. I'd be hard pressed to point to any metaphor in the story that wasn't a cliche, and as a result, the story is trapped at the emotional depth of a LIVE LAUGH LOVE sign rather than developing characters and scenes in a novel way.

Narrative Ending.explanation: No, the ending misses the mark here. The author uses the ending to give us the Big Takeaway rather than any sense of completion or closure.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: No; the story does do a good job of slowing down to describe the visit itself, but the narrator spends so much time focused on giving us Meaning that it works against what strengths might exist for the story otherwise.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: No, but this criterion was tricky for me for this story. To be sure, this isn't good writing, but there is an obvious, concerted effort on the part of the writer to balance scene and summary. The sticking point for me, though, comes down to process versus product: It seems clear to me as a reader that the writer is well aware of the need to find the right balance for a particular story as it relates to summary/exposition and scene, but that's a matter of craft not yet borne out in the text, and the product/story itself shows that the writer isn't quite up to the task yet.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: No, the story doesn't offer the reader any actual turns here. I think this is, in part at least, due to the fact that it's super hard to care what happens to these characters. Maybe that's just me being ornery, but all the tuna sandwiches and crossword puzzles in the world can't salvage, for me, the story since it's devoid of what would pass for real human emotion. There's nothing unexpected here, making even the specifics offered feel washed out and insignificant.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: No, there's nothing diverse about any perspectives here. Maybe the mother would offer something of importance or connection? but because this is a world filtered through this frankly unbearable narrator, we'll never know.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: No. Everything that happens externally seems created by the author to give the narrator a reason to reminisce, and by a few paragraph in to the story, it becomes somewhat maddening.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: No, there's not originality in structure, language, style, genre, or format, as far as I can tell. The story is told in a super linear fashion, and the writing itself doesn't offer anything memorable in terms of innovative style or voice.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: No, there's nothing unusual or original here to be had. Somehow, the story manages to miss the mark on all the criteria for lasting impact--it neither entertains, informs, provokes thought, challenges beliefs, provides comfort, not raises awareness. The story, in fact, seems hostile toward taking on novel or original ideas, luxuriating instead in the tried and true cliche of narrative and language.

Originality in Thought.explanation: No, and this is the element of the story that produces the most ire in me because it's clear that there's *something* the writer is trying to do in this story! But whether it's the "lifetime of shared moments and cherished summer afternoons," the horrible "vintage peppermint-stick candy in its window," or the familiarity that "[wrapped] itself around me like a cozy blanket," the writer settles for the well-worn path of cliche at EVERY opportunity. To quote the narrator, "My heart shattered into a thousand pieces.

World Building and Setting.explanation: No. First, I must say that it's in the specifics offered that the story gains any traction at all; although by the ending I find the same ol' specifics tedious, upon first mention, sentences like "| made us tuna salad sandwiches, heavy on the pickles, while Mom set out glasses of iced tea garnished with mint from her garden" give the illusion of a real world in some form or fashion. Additionally, the narrative seems almost entirely controlled by a weird obsession with food; every event or action is described through an organizing feature of whatever twee meal they prepared and enjoyed together. It's unsettling.

Character Development.explanation: No, and I'm sure by this point in the response, the rationale is obvious: The story as a whole feels in service of Teaching Someone About Nostalgia, and as a result, the characters become pawns created only to further this agenda.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: No, here again, there's only a smidge of meaning offered even at the surface level since these characters feel too quaint to be real, so the possibility for subtext is entirely off the table, I'm afraid.
